body:
Fixes #10506

Value nodes cached their lazily formatted UTF-8 text in a 32-byte `ReadOnlyMemorySegment` field. That write is not atomic, so two threads reading a node for the first time could see a half-written segment and get an empty literal, which surfaced as SDL like `@constraint(minLength: )`.

This PR publishes every lazily computed value through a single reference or a volatile flag. `IntValueNode` formats in its constructor and parses on conversion. `FloatValueNode` keeps one inline `double` and a volatile state byte: a node built from text caches the parsed double behind the state, a node built from a `double` formats its text lazily and publishes it behind the state, and a node built from a `decimal` formats eagerly. `StringValueNode` publishes its encoded bytes behind a volatile flag. `EnumValueNode` keeps its string in one reference field and swaps in a small holder with the string and its UTF-8 bytes once encoded. No node is larger than on `main`.

## Benchmarks

The float and string rows for a new text node and the enum `AsSpan()` rows were re-measured after def4ec3995, which trims the text constructors and lets `EnumValueNode.AsSpan()` inline, with `main` and the PR in the same session. Every other row is from the original pass.

**Verdict:** a net improvement. On the hot path, Hot Chocolate coerces each integer variable 32% faster with 46% less allocation, because the node no longer allocates a `byte[]` on its first conversion, and Fusion forwards each integer variable 8 B smaller at the same speed. Cost analysis reads literal slicing arguments as doubles 5 times faster, because the text is parsed as a `long` first. A reused node parses its text on every conversion, which costs about 1 ns more per call and only reaches the hot path for arguments that mix literals and variables. Building a node from an `int` costs 2.5 ns more because the text is formatted eagerly, and allocates 16 B less; printing or forwarding such a node is 2 to 3 times faster. The reused `ToUInt64()` row is an artifact of the long pass: the out-of-process pass measured 2.07 ns against 0.89 ns on `main`, in line with the other widths.
